cards.front: How does North Carolina law treat bicycles, and which laws must bicyclists obey?
cards.back: North Carolina law treats bicycles as vehicles, so bicyclists must obey the same traffic laws as drivers, including the DWI laws.

cards.front: Where should drivers expect bicyclists, and when may a bicyclist use the full lane?
cards.back: Drivers should expect bicyclists in the roadway, and traffic conditions may require a bicyclist to use the full travel lane.

cards.front: Where may bicyclists ride, and what guides their choice?
cards.back: Bicyclists may ride in a bike lane, on a paved shoulder or in a regular travel lane, choosing based on road conditions, hazards and conflicts with right-turning cars.

cards.front: Which driver duties also apply to bicyclists?
cards.back: Like drivers, bicyclists must ride on the right side of the road, stop for stop signs and red lights, and give hand signals.

cards.front: How should you pass a bicyclist, and what is the safest way?
cards.back: Pass a bicyclist only with plenty of clearance and no oncoming traffic in the other lane; changing lanes is the safest way to pass.

cards.front: Which laws govern passing a bicyclist?
cards.back: Passing a bicyclist lawfully means following the same vehicle passing laws that apply to passing any other vehicle.

cards.front: Which way should bicyclists ride relative to traffic, and why?
cards.back: Bicyclists should ride with the flow of traffic, never facing it, because drivers often fail to look toward a wrong-way rider.

cards.front: Where should you expect bicycles, and which collisions should you watch for?
cards.back: Expect bicycles on every road except where they are expressly banned, and watch for left-cross, drive-out and right-hook collisions.

cards.front: What lights must a bicycle have at night, and how far must they be visible?
cards.back: At night a bicycle must have a front light visible from at least three hundred feet and a rear red light or reflector visible from at least two hundred feet.

cards.front: How do the front and rear bicycle light distances differ?
cards.back: A bicycle at night needs a front light seen from three hundred feet but a rear red light or reflector seen from only two hundred feet.

cards.front: Who must wear an approved bicycle helmet?
cards.back: Every bicycle rider and passenger under age sixteen must wear an approved bicycle helmet and sit on a saddle seat.

cards.front: Which bicycle passengers must ride in a restraining seat?
cards.back: A bicycle passenger under forty pounds or under forty inches tall must ride in a bicycle restraining seat.

cards.front: How does the helmet rule's limit differ from the restraining seat rule's limit?
cards.back: The bicycle helmet rule covers riders and passengers under sixteen, while the restraining seat rule covers passengers under forty pounds or forty inches.
cards.memory_hook: helmet by age, seat by size

cards.front: How does the pedestrian share of crash deaths differ between cities and rural areas?
cards.back: In cities about two of every five people killed in motor vehicle crashes are pedestrians, compared with about one in ten in rural areas.

cards.front: Where do pedestrians make up the larger share of crash deaths?
cards.back: Pedestrians make up about two of every five crash deaths in cities but only about one in ten in rural areas.

cards.front: Who are most of the pedestrians killed?
cards.back: Most pedestrians killed are children, elderly people or people who had been drinking.

cards.front: Which side of the road should pedestrians walk on, and what should they wear?
cards.back: Pedestrians should walk on the left side of the road facing traffic and wear or carry something white.

cards.front: What should you carry and be ready to do when walking at night?
cards.back: On foot at night, carry a flashlight and be ready to step aside, since drivers may not see you.

cards.front: How does the pedestrian walking direction differ from the bicyclist riding direction?
cards.back: Pedestrians walk on the left facing traffic, which is the opposite of the ride-with-traffic rule for bicyclists.

cards.front: How do heavy trucks gain speed, and how can their size mislead you?
cards.back: Heavy trucks gain speed slowly, especially uphill, and their size can make them seem slower than they really are.

cards.front: Why does a truck need extra room to turn, and what should you check before passing?
cards.back: A truck's rear wheels do not follow its front wheels, so it needs extra room to turn; check its turn signal before passing a truck that seems to start a left turn.

cards.front: What happens to truck brakes on downhill runs?
cards.back: Truck brakes heat up on downhill runs, which means the truck needs more distance to stop.

cards.front: How can a large truck beside you affect your steering?
cards.back: Wind currents from a large truck beside you can affect your steering, so give trucks plenty of room.

cards.front: What false assumption do drivers make about how high truck drivers sit?
cards.back: Truck drivers sit about twice as high as car drivers, but it is a false assumption that they can see everything around them.

cards.front: Where are a tractor-trailer's no-zones?
cards.back: A tractor-trailer's no-zones reach up to twenty feet in front of the cab, along both sides especially beside the cab, and up to two hundred feet behind.

cards.front: How does the front no-zone compare with the rear no-zone?
cards.back: A truck's front no-zone extends up to twenty feet, but its rear no-zone extends up to two hundred feet.

cards.front: Why should you not linger in a truck's no-zone, and what is the mirror test?
cards.back: Lingering in a truck's no-zone makes it harder for the trucker to steer clear of danger; if you cannot see the driver in the side mirror, the driver cannot see you.

cards.front: How do recreational vehicles differ from cars in size and handling?
cards.back: Recreational vehicles are typically longer, higher and wider than cars, speed up and stop more slowly, and need more turning room.

cards.front: How does following close behind a recreational vehicle affect your view?
cards.back: The closer you get to a recreational vehicle, the more it blocks your view, and its driver has much larger blind spots than a car driver.

cards.front: What should you watch for near a vehicle towing a trailer?
cards.back: Near a vehicle towing a trailer, watch for sway in crosswinds or on slippery curves, and know that sudden braking can make the trailer jackknife.

cards.front: How much clear road may passing a trailer and its towing vehicle take?
cards.back: Passing a trailer and its towing vehicle safely can take a half mile of clear road.

cards.front: What two facts should you remember about passing and braking near a trailer?
cards.back: Passing a vehicle towing a trailer may need a half mile of clear road, and braking hard near it risks a jackknife.

cards.front: What right-of-way consideration do motorcycle and moped riders get?
cards.back: Give motorcycle and moped riders the same right-of-way consideration as any other driver.

cards.front: How do you pass a motorcycle?
cards.back: A motorcycle is entitled to its full lane, so pass it by changing lanes exactly as you would for a larger vehicle.

cards.front: Where do mopeds ride in the lane, and how much room must you leave when passing?
cards.back: Mopeds ride on the right side of the lane, and when passing one you must stay at least two feet to its left.

cards.front: How does passing a motorcycle differ from passing a moped?
cards.back: To pass a motorcycle you change lanes because it owns its full lane, while to pass a moped you keep at least two feet to its left.

cards.front: Why leave extra room when passing any cyclist?
cards.back: Leave enough room when passing any cyclist so your vehicle's windstream cannot make the rider lose control.

cards.front: When should you look especially for motorcycles and mopeds?
cards.back: Motorcycles and mopeds can be completely hidden in blind spots, so look for them before turning, changing lanes or pulling out, especially when turning left.

cards.front: In motorcycle crashes involving a car, who is usually at fault?
cards.back: About two-thirds of North Carolina motorcycle crashes involve a car, and in most of them the car driver is at fault, often saying the motorcycle went unseen.

cards.front: How does motorcycle stopping compare with car stopping?
cards.back: Most motorcycles stop faster than cars, but they stop more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces where hard braking could cause a fall.

cards.front: When do motorcycles stop more slowly than usual?
cards.back: Motorcycles usually stop faster than cars, but more slowly with a passenger or on poor road surfaces.

cards.front: Which surface hazards can upset a rider ahead, and what does a wobbling rider suggest?
cards.back: Sand, gravel, wet leaves or water on the pavement can make a rider ahead lose control, and a wobbling or hesitant rider is likely a beginner who needs extra room.

cards.front: How much room should you give a motorcycle or moped on slippery roads?
cards.back: Never crowd a motorcycle or moped, and leave a longer following distance on slippery roads because two wheels are easily destabilized.

cards.front: Where should you give riders extra room?
cards.back: Give riders extra room at railroad crossings, on rough roads and on metal surfaces such as steel bridge joints and grating.

cards.front: What helmet must moped riders and passengers wear?
cards.back: Moped riders and all passengers must wear a helmet meeting Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard two hundred eighteen with the retention strap fastened.

cards.front: How does North Carolina define a moped?
cards.back: North Carolina defines a moped as a two- or three-wheeled vehicle with a motor of no more than fifty cubic centimeters and no external shifting device.

cards.front: What is a moped's top speed limit, and what about faster models?
cards.back: A moped's top speed may not exceed thirty miles per hour, and mopeds built to go faster are illegal to use in North Carolina.

cards.front: What does a moped operator need to ride on a public road?
cards.back: To operate a moped on a public road you must be at least sixteen and hold a valid N.C. driver license or ID card, and impaired driving laws apply to moped riders too.

cards.front: What are the three moped limits for motor, speed and operator age?
cards.back: A moped is limited to a motor of fifty cubic centimeters and a top speed of thirty miles per hour, and its operator must be at least sixteen.

cards.front: How should moped riders position themselves in traffic?
cards.back: Moped riders should keep right in the lane, never share a lane with another vehicle, and never squeeze between parked cars and moving traffic at an intersection.

cards.front: What should moped riders wear and use to be seen?
cards.back: Moped riders should wear light or bright clothing and use electric turn signals if fitted, or hand signals otherwise.

cards.front: What must every moped have since registration became required?
cards.back: Since July two thousand fifteen, every moped must be registered with the DMV and display a license plate on the rear at all times.

cards.front: What can a moped owner use as proof of ownership without the certificate of origin?
cards.back: A moped owner without the manufacturer's certificate of origin can use form MVR-fifty-eight, an affidavit of facts, as proof of ownership.

cards.front: What do moped registration and the ownership affidavit have in common?
cards.back: Moped registration has been required since July two thousand fifteen, and an owner lacking the certificate of origin may file form MVR-fifty-eight instead.

cards.front: Who is held responsible when litter comes from a vehicle?
cards.back: Littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle.

cards.front: How does the fine for a first littering conviction differ from a repeat?
cards.back: A first littering conviction is fined two hundred fifty dollars to one thousand dollars, while a repeat within three years is fined five hundred dollars to two thousand dollars.

recap_hooks.text: Bicycles are vehicles; expect them in the lane, even using the full lane.
Pass a bicyclist with plenty of room, ideally by changing lanes.
Bicycles need a front light and a rear red light or reflector at night.
Helmets go by age; restraining seats go by size.
Pedestrians are a bigger share of crash deaths in cities than in rural areas.
Pedestrians walk on the left facing traffic, unlike bicyclists.
Trucks need room to turn and to stop downhill.
Stay out of the no-zones; the rear zone is the longest.
Recreational vehicles block your view and need more room.
Trailers can sway or jackknife and take a long stretch to pass.
Change lanes to pass a motorcycle; leave room when passing a moped.
Look for riders hidden in blind spots, especially turning left.
Motorcycles stop more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces.
Never crowd a rider, and give extra room on rough or metal surfaces.
Mopeds have motor, speed and operator age limits.
Mopeds must be registered and show a rear plate.
Littering is illegal, and the driver is responsible.
A repeat littering conviction carries a higher fine.
